extracted.intended_audience: artists, art theorists, literary critics, and students of aesthetics/philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and tests for judging works of art and the aesthetic disposition of mind: what constitutes aesthetic excellence, how art should affect the spectator, and the educational/moral role of aesthetic experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic freedom (the medium situation)
rubrics_metrics.description: “This medium situation in which the soul is neither physically nor morally constrained, and yet is in both ways active, merits essentially the name of a free situation...that state of real and active determination should be called the aesthetic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic excellence requires a balance in which sensibility and reason are simultaneously active, neutralizing their exclusive determinative powers. The aesthetic state is the intermediary that allows a sensuous person to regain determinability and pass into active thought and will; works should enable this free intermediate state rather than enforce sensuous or moral determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form should dominate; substance be inoperative
rubrics_metrics.description: “In a really beautiful work of art, the substance ought to be inoperative, the form should do everything; for by the form the whole man is acted on; the substance acts on nothing but isolated forces.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic success is measured by the ability of form to neutralize the limiting, particular effects of subject-matter. The artist’s task is to ‘destroy matter by the form’ so that even an imposing or attractive subject does not force a narrow, determinate response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / unlimited character of disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Any class of productions or separate work in the world of art is noble and excellent in proportion to the universality of the disposition and the unlimited character of the bias thereby presented to our mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work’s nobility depends on how widely it opens the spectator’s disposition (universality) rather than fixing it into a particular bias. Excellence is judged by how little a work confines the mind to a single, limited mode of feeling or thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-didacticism / anti-didactic requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: “The idea of an instructive fine art (didactic art) or improving (moral) art is no less contradictory, for nothing agrees less with the idea of the beautiful than to give a determinate tendency to the mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True aesthetic effect must not aim to produce a determinate moral or intellectual result. Didactic or overtly moralizing art violates the aesthetic principle by imposing a determinate tendency on the spectator’s mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emancipation from the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The infallible effect of the beautiful is emancipation from the passions. The idea of an impassioned fine art is a contradiction in terms.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic excellence consists in liberating the spectator from being dominated by passions; even works that portray strong passion should preserve the spectator’s freedom rather than inflame or entrap the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elasticity / freedom to shift modes (test of purity)
rubrics_metrics.description: “This high indifference and freedom of mind, united with power and elasticity, is the disposition in which a true work of art ought to dismiss us... If after an enjoyment of this kind we find ourselves specially impelled to a particular mode of feeling or action... we have not experienced any pure aesthetic effect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical test of pure aesthetic effect: after experiencing the work one should be capable of easily shifting from grave to gay, rest to movement, submission to resistance, etc. If the work leaves you locked into a particular mood or disposition, it has failed the test of aesthetic purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation to an ideal of aesthetic purity
rubrics_metrics.description: “As in reality no purely aesthetical effect can be met with... the excellence of a work of art can only consist in its greater approximation to its ideal of aesthetic purity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because complete aesthetic purity is unattainable in human life, works are evaluated by degree: how closely they approach the ideal of indeterminate, universal form. The closer a work comes to this ideal (while still operating within human limits), the higher its aesthetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendence of medium-specific limits (perfect style)
rubrics_metrics.description: “In each art, the perfect style consists exactly in knowing how to remove specific limits, while sacrificing at the same time the particular advantages of the art, and to give it by a wise use of what belongs to it specially a more general character.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great works tend to transcend their medium’s particular affinities (e.g., music’s sensuousness, sculpture’s determinacy) and approximate other arts’ effects. Perfect style balances losing some medium-specific advantage to gain a more universal, general effect on the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of trivial or passionate subjects so as to preserve freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most frivolous subject ought to be treated in such a way that we preserve the faculty to exchange it immediately for the most serious work... The arts which have passion for their object... do not present a difficulty here... even in this class a work is perfect in proportion as amidst the most violent storms of passion it respects the liberty of the soul.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An artist must handle any subject—even frivolous or passionate material—so that the spectator’s mental freedom remains intact. The measure of perfection is the capacity to treat strong or trivial matter without imposing a lasting determinate bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer’s aesthetic disposition matters (taste and perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: “If his mind is too stretched or too relaxed... it will only stop to look at the parts, and it will only see matter in the most beautiful form... The interest he takes in the work is either solely moral or exclusively physical; the only thing wanting to it is to be exactly what it ought to be--aesthetical.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments about a work must account for the observer’s habitual mode of reception: some viewers will focus on matter or morals rather than form because of their dispositions. Critical evaluation should differentiate defects of the work from limitations in the spectator’s taste or training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic disposition as necessary for moral and intellectual development
rubrics_metrics.description: “By the aesthetic disposition of the soul the proper activity of reason is already revealed in the sphere of sensuousness... The transition from an aesthetic state to a logical and moral state... is then infinitely more easy... One of the most important tasks of culture is to submit man to form... and to render it aesthetic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic education is judged by its capacity to restore human freedom and to prepare the individual for moral autonomy and rational judgment. Art’s educational value is not in teaching specific truths or duties, but in cultivating the freedom and form required for moral and intellectual life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as sphere of unfettered contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Beauty is indeed the sphere of unfettered contemplation and reflection; beauty conducts us into the world of ideas, without however taking us from the world of sense.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic value includes the ability to enable contemplative reflection (access to ideas) while remaining connected to sensible experience. Works should open the mind to ideas without forcibly converting the spectator to purely intellectual or purely sensuous modes.
